front: FCFF from CFO (interest paid in CFO)
back: FCFF = CFO + Int(1 − t) − FCInv. Cash available to all capital providers after investment.
FCFE = CFO − FCInv + Net borrowing, where net borrowing = debt issued − debt repaid. Also FCFE = FCFF − Int(1 − t) + net borrowing.
FCFF = NI + NCC + Int(1 − t) − FCInv − WCInv.

front: FCFF from EBIT and from EBITDA
back: From EBIT: EBIT(1 − t) + Dep − FCInv − WCInv. From EBITDA: EBITDA(1 − t) + Dep × t − FCInv − WCInv.

front: Two methods of common-size cash flow statements
back: Inflows/outflows method: each item as a % of total inflows or total outflows. Revenue method: each item as a % of net revenue.
CFO/revenue; CFO/average total assets (cash return on assets); CFO/average equity (cash return on equity); CFO/operating income (cash to income); (CFO − preferred dividends)/weighted average shares.

front: Debt coverage and interest coverage ratios
back: Debt coverage = CFO ÷ total debt. Interest coverage = (CFO + interest paid + taxes paid) ÷ interest paid.

front: Reinvestment, debt payment and dividend payment ratios
back: Reinvestment = CFO ÷ cash paid for long-term assets. Debt payment = CFO ÷ cash paid for LT debt repayment. Dividend payment = CFO ÷ dividends paid.
CFO ÷ cash outflows for investing and financing activities. Below 1.0 means CFO alone cannot cover those outflows.

front: What does a cash to income ratio persistently below 1.0 suggest?
back: Operating income is not converting to cash, which may indicate low earnings quality (for example rising receivables or inventory) or heavy working capital investment.

front: Effect of classifying interest paid in financing (IFRS)
back: CFO is higher and CFF lower by the interest paid; total cash change is unchanged. Adjust before comparing CFO-based ratios across companies.
